newsitem.title: GERMANY: Frankfurt punters back Buba in clash with Bonn.
newsitem.headline: Frankfurt punters back Buba in clash with Bonn.

text.p: Punters on the streets of Frankfurt are betting on the Bundsbank to win its clash with the Bonn government over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue the German central bank's gold reserves.

To average Germans, an independent Bundesbank is a kind of knight in shining armour and many are cheering it on as it girds to battle what they see as Bonn's attempt to steamroller through Europes monetary union (EMU) at all costs.

"The politicians only think where their next vote is coming from, not about what's best for the mark in our pockets," said a middle-aged man strolling down the Zeil, the main shopping street in Germany's financial capital.
His wife nodded vigourously, but cautious burghers that they were, they asked not to be named.
Martin Kueppers, a young company executive, had no such inhibition about speaking his mind: "I would definitely be more on the Bundesbank's side in this argument.
"This whole currency union can only work if the politicians stick to the criteria they have set themselves."
The Frankfurt-based Bundesbank last week blasted Bonn for wanting to revalue its gold and currency reserves and use the hidden profits to help whip its finances into shape for EMU.
But Bonn plans to push a draft law through parliament to change the Bundesbank statutes and reap 20 billion marks ($12 billion) in profits to partly ease its budget deficit burden.
The holiday weekend sun brought people out in droves to the Zeil, but opinions were as varied as the flavours of ice cream available to help keep cool from the early summer-like weather.

Some were totally opposed to the euro while others doubted Germany would qualify for it. Some said Bonn must explain why the mark, a symbol of Germany's post-war rebirth, should now be given up for an untested and maybe unstable euro.

The responses reflected a paradox opinion pollsters always point out, namely that two-thirds of Germans oppose EMU but about the same number say they are pro-European and expect the single currency to come anyway. If the mark is doomed, they think, the euro really must be just as stable and strong.
Bettina Traub, a marketing executive with a large U.S. firm, said: "A strong independent Bundesbank is a good idea and it can keep stability going before European monetary union."
"I think the euro is a great idea. I travel a lot for my job -- I've got three different currencies in my pocket right now -- and it is a pain to have to keep changing currencies."
"We have to be careful that this is not seen as accounting trickery," said one elderly man, who asked not to be named.

His generation had lived through World War Two, worked hard for a strong mark and would not give it up easily, he said, adding: "If we are not careful, the mark could end up like the lire, which I don't think is nearly as stable as our mark."
No accounting tricks, but then no EMU without Germany is a common view. The idea of currency union without Germany was generally viewed as a rather preposterous notion.
"They do seem to be pushing it through, which is a bit worrying. But if Germany doesn't join in the initial stages, then it is difficult to see the point of the whole exercise," Traub said.

Added Kueppers: "If Germany doesn't make it then, what is the point. The euro needs to be as strong as the mark. What is missing here is a good marketing campaign. Not enough has been done to explain what the euro will do for us. It's all about creating trust."
